query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Nanoparticles in which the multi‐element solid‐solution state is kinetically frozen via a rapid cooling (quenching) step will preserve their high-entropy, single-phase structure during high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric operation because the limited atomic mobility prevents diffusion-driven phase segregation and coarsening.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles synthesized from a single-source precursor by low-temperature reduction.
generation.intervention: Introduce a rapid quenching step immediately after synthesis (to freeze the atomic configuration) and compare the stability with nanoparticles that undergo conventional slow cooling.
generation.conditions: Nanoparticles are exposed to service conditions (for catalysis: 773–1173 K; for thermoelectric use: 473–1923 K) under controlled atmospheres that mimic the intended application (e.g., inert or reactive gas compositions as required by the catalytic test).
generation.structural_mediator: The kinetically trapped, highly disordered atomic arrangement with limited free atomic mobility that results from a rapid cooling process.
generation.mechanism: Rapid quenching following low-temperature synthesis freezes in the high-entropy solid-solution state by preventing significant atomic diffusion. This inhibition of diffusion suppresses phase segregation and sintering during subsequent high-temperature service, thereby maintaining structural and chemical uniformity even when exposed to temperatures that would otherwise activate atomic mobility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline slowly cooled nanoparticles, the rapidly quenched nanoparticles will retain a more uniform, single-phase structure with limited grain growth, phase separation, or agglomeration when tested under service conditions.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles produced via identical low-temperature reduction but allowed to cool slowly so that increased atomic mobility during cooling promotes some degree of elemental segregation or coarsening.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to near-equiatomic, multi-element nanoparticles prepared by low-temperature, single-source precursor methods. It may not extend to particles synthesized under conditions with inherently high atomic mobility (e.g., high-temperature shock methods) or to systems with significant deviations from near-equiatomic compositions.
generation.uncertainty: The precise extent to which rapid quenching can enhance stability, and how sensitive the outcome is to the specific elemental combinations and service atmospheres, remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two batches of the same multi-element, near-equiatomic nanoparticles using a low-temperature, single-source precursor method. Subject one batch to rapid quenching immediately after synthesis, while the other is allowed to cool slowly. Expose both batches to service conditions (773–1173 K for catalytic operation and/or 473–1923 K for thermoelectric testing) for a predetermined duration and compare the evolution of phase composition, particle size, and elemental distribution using in situ TEM, XRD, and STEM-EDX.
measurements: Functional properties (e.g., catalytic activity or thermoelectric performance)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapidly quenched nanoparticles do not exhibit significantly less phase segregation, sintering, or compositional inhomogeneity than the slowly cooled nanoparticles under identical service conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) are an important new material class with significant application potential in catalysis and electrocatalysis. The entropy-driven formation of HEA materials requires high temperatures and controlled cooling rates. However, catalysts in general also require highly dispersed materials, i.e., nanoparticles. Only then a favorable utilization of the expensive raw materials can be achieved. Several recently reported HEA nanoparticle synthesis strategies, therefore, avoid the high-temperature regime to prevent particle growth. In our work, we investigate a system of five noble metal single-source precursors with superior catalytic activity for the oxygen reduction reaction. Combining in situ X-ray powder diffraction with multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy, we address the fundamental question of how single-phase HEA nanoparticles can form at low temperatures. It is demonstrated that the formation of HEA nanoparticles is governed by stochastic principles and the inhibition of precursor mobility during the formation process favors the formation of a single phase. The proposed formation principle is supported by simulations of the nanoparticle formation

Further in situ annealing studies up to 1173 K also confirms the excellent thermal stability of nanoparticles. We believe the mechanistic details reported in this work would not only guide the nanoparticles synthesis through Joule heating-based methods, but also pave the way on understanding other rapid high temperature synthesis approaches.
